messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 59

Elias first notices the pattern in late autumn. It begins as a misplaced package at his apartment door, then escalates to a familiar sedan idling outside the café where he usually meets his students. He tells himself it is coincidence, then convenience, until a handwritten letter arrives addressed to him at an address he never provided. The words are precise, possessive, and unmistakably real. He files a report with the police, secures a protective order, and tells his wife, Clara, everything. For weeks, he expects the relief that accompanies external validation. Instead, the quiet that follows is heavier than the messages ever were. Spring arrives, but Elias stops stepping outside after sunset. He begins checking the deadbolt four times, listening for the mechanical click to settle in his chest. When he sits at his desk to prepare lesson plans for his high school students, his shoulders instinctively pivot toward the window. He tells himself he is being prudent, but his mind keeps replaying the exact moment the car’s brake lights flared in his rearview. He starts letting his phone ring, then texting back hours later that he cannot speak. His tutoring roster shrinks from ten students to three, all conducted over a laptop with the camera disabled. He tells his students he is streamlining his materials digitally. He does not mention the way his stomach tightens when the doorbell chimes, or how he silently maps every exit when he walks into a bookstore or public library. By summer, exhaustion has settled into his joints. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. without warning, heart hammering, certain he hears boots on the pavement below. He opens his security app out of reflex, watching empty alleys until his eyes burn. Clara asks him to unwind, to let her manage the perimeters, but Elias brushes her off, insisting he needs to stay watchful. He catches himself calculating how long it would take to reach the street from their balcony, whether the neighbors’ routine creates blind spots, how many times he will have to glance over his shoulder. He cancels dinner invitations, tells colleagues he is finishing a manuscript, and stops responding to Clara’s casual remarks. He feels untethered from his own days, as if watching them through frosted glass, yet his nerves remain drawn taut, braced for the next notification, the next unfamiliar face, the next boundary crossed. Today, Elias teaches from a corner of his home office, the blinds drawn to a narrow, calculated slit. He has relearned how to walk students through integral calculus while simultaneously muting browser alerts, archiving old emails, and resisting the urge to refresh his inbox. He knows he should feel secure now. The legal paperwork is signed. The known numbers are blocked. Yet when a student pauses mid-question, his attention drifts to the way rain streaks the window, imagining the droplets trace a pattern he once knew too well. He closes his notebook when the hour ends, pours a glass of water he does not finish, and watches the street through the gap in the slats. His fingers tremble, then flatten against the desk. He tells himself this is simply how the days will pass until the weight lifts. He does not know when it will, but he continues to show up, session by session, alertness by alertness, breath by breath.
